chapters.title: Why it really ended (your side of it)
chapters.teaser: Not who was right. What your soul was doing while it fell apart.

chapters.title: Your breakup pattern
chapters.teaser: How you end things, how you grieve, and the habit that slows you down.

chapters.title: Why you keep checking
chapters.teaser: What the pull back toward them is really asking for.

chapters.title: So, will they come back? The honest answer
chapters.teaser: What a chart can and can't tell you, and the question that matters more.

chapters.title: If they ever reach out
chapters.teaser: Three questions to ask before you reply, built for your soul.

chapters.title: What you do now
chapters.teaser: The next small steps that help, whatever they decide.

text.why-it-ended: Jeong Fire is the candle: intimate, focused, the light people sit close to. You love with intensity and pay attention to tiny things, a shift in tone, a reply that came later than usual. That sensitivity makes you a deep partner. It also means you probably noticed the ending long before anyone said it, and maybe you started grieving while you were still in it. Candle types read meaning into small silences and then protect themselves by pulling back first. If this breakup felt like a slow flicker rather than a crash, that's why. Ask yourself honestly: what did I feel early, and did I ever say it out loud?
text.your-breakup-pattern: You hold a breakup close. Jeong Fire doesn't announce, it processes, privately and thoroughly, usually around two in the morning. You might analyse every message, reread old notes, build careful theories. You're looking for the meaning, because meaning makes pain bearable. The trap is that thinking about it starts to feel like still being in it. Your other pattern is loyalty to the memory: you keep a little flame lit long after the other person has left the room. That flame is beautiful. It's also yours to set down when your hands get tired.
text.the-pull: What pulls you back is intimacy. You let very few people into the small, warm room where your real self lives, and they were in there. Losing that access feels like part of you went dark. Of course you want it back. But the room is still yours. It never belonged to them. Let someone else in, even a little: a friend who's good at deep talks, a sibling, a journal you actually keep. What you need is closeness, and closeness can be rebuilt, slowly, with people who've earned a seat by the candle.
text.the-honest-answer: Nobody can tell you what's happening inside someone else's heart, and your chart doesn't hold their choices. It does hold yours. Jeong Fire tends to fixate, letting one person become the only light in the room. If you want them back, ask whether you want them, or the feeling of being deeply known. Ask too whether you felt safe being fully yourself with them, moods included. If the honest answer is mixed, the work isn't winning them back. It's learning to say what you feel while you feel it, so the next ending, if there ever is one, surprises nobody.
text.if-they-reach-out: If they reach out, you'll read the message twelve times and decode every comma. Breathe first. Then read it once more as if a friend had sent it to you. What does it actually say? Jeong Fire's intuition is strong, but in heartbreak it can run on fear instead of facts. Reply when you're calm, and not at night. Say one true thing about how you feel, and watch how they handle it. Someone worth reconnecting with can hold your honesty. Someone who flinches from it was probably part of why the light flickered to begin with.
text.what-you-do-now: Protect your flame. Jeong Fire burns best in calm rooms, so build some calm. Sleep before midnight when you can. Leave the phone in another room at night. Light an actual candle if you like the ritual. Spend time on something that rewards focus: writing, drawing, slow cooking, learning one deep thing properly. Choose two or three people and tell them more than you usually would. And when the urge to analyse arrives, give it a time limit. Twenty minutes, then close the notebook. You were never only someone's light. You're your own.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: You noticed everything, Jeong. That's how deeply you loved.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: You also saw the ending months early and said nothing. Classic.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Your 2am feelings are real, but they're not the whole truth.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Read their message once. Not twelve times. Once.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Let a friend into the warm room for a while.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Your flame is yours. Stop handing matches to people who left.

spring.intro: A candle lit in spring has wood stacked all around it. Wood commanded your birth season, Jeong, and Wood feeds Fire, so your inner flame is well supplied with feeling, memory and care. You love with focus: one person, fully seen. That's why this breakup hurts in such detail. You remember the song in the car, the exact wording of that text, the way they said your name. Your fuel is memory itself, and right now you're burning it to keep warm. It works until it doesn't. The spring candle's gift is renewal. You can light from fresh wood: new friends, new rooms, new stories. You don't have to keep burning the old ones.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: You're using old texts as firewood. That supply runs out, Jeong.

summer.intro: A candle in midsummer is a candle in a room full of other flames. Fire ruled your season, Jeong, so your chart carries a lot of your own element, which makes you intense, loyal and quietly fierce. In love you probably gave everything to a small circle of two. When it ended, the heat had nowhere to go. You might be burning it as anger, or as hours of analysis, or as a playlist you can't stop replaying. Summer Jeong can mistake intensity for meaning: it hurts this much, so it must be the one. Not necessarily. Sometimes it hurts this much because you're built to burn steadily. Let the flame settle before you read anything into it.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: It hurting this much doesn't make them the one. You just burn hot.

autumn.intro: Autumn Jeong is the candle in the jeweller's workshop, the precise flame that shapes metal. Metal was in command when you were born, and Fire works on Metal, so your love is attentive and crafted. You noticed details, got things just right, remembered something they mentioned once in March. In the relationship you might have spent your flame refining someone who didn't want reshaping, or refining yourself to fit them. The breakup leaves you holding all that careful work. It wasn't wasted. It's a skill, and it belongs to you. The pull back is wanting the craft to have counted. It did. It doesn't need their approval to be real.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: All that care you crafted? Still yours. It goes wherever you go.

winter.intro: A candle in winter matters more than any other light. Water ruled your birth season, Jeong, and Water puts out Fire, so you grew up protecting your flame from drafts. That's why you trust slowly and love deeply once you do. In the relationship you probably cupped your hands around them. After the breakup, the draft got in. You may feel unusually small and flickery right now, and you might be checking their accounts as if hunting for the window that let the cold in. You won't find a full answer there. Winter candles survive inside a lantern: steady people, routines, warm places. Build yours before you go looking for anyone's draft.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Feeling flickery is allowed. Let your people be the lantern for a while.

strength.strong: Your candle has plenty of fuel, Jeong, which makes your love intense, focused and very hard to switch off. You commit with your whole flame. In a breakup that becomes fixation: analysing, remembering, holding the light up to every detail. You might have pushed for answers they couldn't give. The blind spot is that a steady flame can feel like a spotlight to the person in it. If you're tempted to reach out, check whether you want them or want the story finished. Some stories end mid-sentence. You're allowed to close the book anyway.
strength.weak: Your flame doesn't get much support in your chart, Jeong, so you protect it carefully and give it away even more carefully. Once you chose them, you probably gave more than you kept. You tended their moods, remembered their needs, apologised first. After the breakup you might feel guttered out, as if you used all your light on someone else. You didn't. A small flame relights easily when it's sheltered. Choose people who cup their hands around you too. Your care is precious. It shouldn't cost you all your warmth.

balance_text.too_much_wood: Too much Wood means you push for growth and answers, even in heartbreak. You want a plan for getting over it, maybe even a plan for getting them back. Slow down. Not everything grows on schedule, and some things need to just sit for a while. Ask for help instead of turning healing into a project. For balance, let a little Metal in: declutter, finish old things, clear out the drafts folder. A clean edge helps Wood stop reaching for what's already gone.
balance_text.missing_wood: Missing Wood means fresh starts feel heavy. After a breakup you might stay in the same place, emotionally and literally, for longer than you'd like. That isn't weakness. It just means new growth needs a nudge. Small steps work best: a new route to work, one new class, one new person a week. Get outside in the mornings and keep something green near you. You don't need a whole new life. You need one new branch, and then another.
balance_text.too_much_fire: Too much Fire makes you feel everything at full volume. A breakup can feel like an emergency, with urges to text, post, or fix it all tonight. Your passion is real, but heat isn't a strategy. Before any big move, sleep on it. Cool down with water: swimming, long showers, quiet evenings at home. Talk to your calmest friend before your most exciting one. Let the fire warm you instead of burning through your peace.
balance_text.missing_fire: Missing Fire means joy and visibility don't come easily, and after a breakup you might go dim for a while, hiding from people and from fun. Turn the lights back on gently. Sunshine, music, dancing in the kitchen, one social plan a week even when you'd rather stay in. Letting people see you is the medicine here. Warmth doesn't only live in romance. It's in friends, in laughter, in simply being out in the world.
balance_text.too_much_earth: Too much Earth means you hold on: to routines, to memories, to the hope that things will settle back into their old place. Stability is your gift, but in heartbreak it can turn into staying stuck. Shake the ground a little. Move the furniture, take a short trip, try something unplanned. Let some Wood energy in, growth and new beginnings. You can keep what was good and still leave room for something new to grow.
balance_text.missing_earth: Missing Earth means life can feel unsteady, and a breakup can knock away what little ground you had. You might feel scattered, unsure where to put your feet. Build structure gently: regular meals, a steady bedtime, one place at home that's only yours. Cook something. Walk somewhere. Lean on the people who are reliable. Stability first, big decisions later. You need solid ground under you before deciding anything about the past.
balance_text.too_much_metal: Too much Metal makes you sharp and decisive, sometimes too quickly. You may have cut the relationship off cleanly and then refused to look at what you feel. Or you judge yourself harshly for every mistake you made in it. Soften the edges. Let Water in: rest, tears, music, journaling. Feeling the grief isn't the same as reopening the door. You can keep your boundaries firm and still let your heart thaw.
balance_text.missing_metal: Missing Metal means boundaries are hard, so after a breakup you might keep the door half open, answer every message, or stay friends when it hurts. Practise clean edges. Mute without guilt. Box up their things. Say no without explaining. White and silver, tidy spaces and finished tasks all help your chart. A boundary isn't cold. It's how you protect the part of you that's still healing.
balance_text.too_much_water: Too much Water means you think and feel deeply, maybe endlessly. After a breakup you might drift through memories, analyse every detail, and lose sleep to what-ifs. Your intuition is a gift, but it needs riverbanks. Add some Earth: routines, cooking, walks, people who ground you. Give overthinking a time limit. Feel it fully, then get up and do one ordinary thing.
balance_text.missing_water: Missing Water means rest and reflection get skipped. You may rush past the breakup, staying busy so you never have to sit with it. That works until suddenly it doesn't. Build in quiet on purpose: slow mornings, water by your bed, a few lines in a journal at night, a bath instead of another plan. Let yourself feel without fixing. Intuition grows when you give it some silence.

too_much_wood.speaker: yeon
too_much_wood.text: So much Wood. You've drafted three versions of 'hey, random but' already.

too_much_wood.speaker: bom
too_much_wood.text: That growing energy wants a goal. Give it your own plans, not their inbox.

too_much_fire.speaker: yeon
too_much_fire.text: Too much Fire: every feeling is a five-alarm emergency. It's a breakup, not an inferno.

too_much_fire.speaker: bom
too_much_fire.text: Your passion is beautiful. Let it cool before you hit send on anything.

too_much_earth.speaker: yeon
too_much_earth.text: Heavy Earth. You'd still be in that relationship purely out of habit.

too_much_earth.speaker: bom
too_much_earth.text: Your loyalty is rare. Just make sure you're loyal to yourself too.

too_much_metal.speaker: yeon
too_much_metal.text: Lots of Metal. You cut them off cleanly, then reread everything at midnight.

too_much_metal.speaker: bom
too_much_metal.text: Being firm protected you. Being gentle with yourself will heal you.

too_much_water.speaker: yeon
too_much_water.text: Overflowing Water: you've cried to three songs and written a novel in your notes app.

too_much_water.speaker: bom
too_much_water.text: Feeling deeply is a gift. Just come up for air sometimes.

missing_wood.speaker: bom
missing_wood.text: Missing Wood can make moving on feel stuck. Small new routines count as growth.

missing_wood.speaker: yeon
missing_wood.text: You haven't changed anything since the breakup, including your lock screen. Start there.

missing_fire.speaker: bom
missing_fire.text: Missing Fire can make joy feel far away. Borrow some from a loud friend.

missing_fire.speaker: yeon
missing_fire.text: You stopped having fun when they left. Fun was never theirs to take.

missing_earth.speaker: bom
missing_earth.text: Missing Earth can make everything feel unsteady. Simple routines will hold you.

missing_earth.speaker: yeon
missing_earth.text: No Earth, no anchor. You re-decide whether to text them every hour.

missing_metal.speaker: bom
missing_metal.text: Missing Metal makes boundaries tricky. You're allowed to say no to your own phone.

missing_metal.speaker: yeon
missing_metal.text: No Metal means you'll answer at 2am. Put the phone in another room.

missing_water.speaker: bom
missing_water.text: Missing Water can make grief hide. It's okay to let it surface slowly.

missing_water.speaker: yeon
missing_water.text: You said you're fine twelve times today. Water would like a word.

gap-wood.title: The oak and the March grudge
gap-wood.text: You loved someone who said 'sounds good' and meant it completely, and somehow that was never quite enough. Your Gap Wood ex was solid, upright, generous in big ways: they showed up, they carried things, they made plans. But they texted like a calendar, and you are someone who reads punctuation like tea leaves. You noticed the shorter replies. You noticed they never asked a follow-up. You didn't say so, because saying it felt needy, so you held it, and held it, until a small thing set the whole stack alight and they stared at you like the fire came from nowhere. To them, it did. Here is the sting: you were hurting in a language they didn't speak, and you never translated. When you were upset, they tried to fix it, which felt like being handled. What pulls you back is the safety. With them, you never once wondered if they'd turn up. One thing to try: write down the three things you never said, plainly, as if to a friend. Not to send. To prove to yourself they were sayable. Then say things like that in the week they happen.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Jeong, they weren't psychic. You needed to say it in March, not October.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Gap, one warm detail per text. That's all the candle needed.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Two good people, one missing translator.

eul-wood.title: Flowers by candlelight, never said aloud
eul-wood.text: You loved a vine, which means you loved someone whose attention spread across a whole garden of friends while you wanted it gathered in one place, on you. Your Eul Wood ex was tender and romantic. Long messages, late-night feelings, the way they read your moods. But they went vague when something was wrong, and you went quiet, and two people politely not saying things can fill a flat with smoke. When they made plans with friends, you felt the flame flicker, and when you asked where they'd been, they felt watched. You worried together, which only made the worries bigger. You gave focused, total love, and it felt like it was being spread thin in return. That's painful, and it's also worth looking at, because focus can tip into possession without you noticing. You felt deeply understood in the quiet moments, and that's what tugs. What helps is building a life with more than one candle in it. Friends, a project, an evening that belongs only to you. Love feels less frightening when it isn't the only light in the room.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Jeong, your love was real. It just needed more than one person to hold it.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Eul, 'it's nothing' was never nothing. You both knew.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Agree on a code word for 'I'm actually upset.' Then actually use it.

byeong-fire.title: The sun and the candle in different rooms
byeong-fire.text: You loved the sun and wanted it to shine only in your room. That's not a crime; it's what candles do. Your Byeong Fire ex was warm with everyone: the barista, the group chat, the friend of a friend at the party. You sent fewer, deeper messages and watched them reply to five other people first. You felt like one of the many. They felt your focus as weight. Arguments were quick and hot, the two of you flaring at once, and they forgot by breakfast while you kept the details for weeks, filed and annotated. That's the wound: you remembered, they didn't, and it made you feel you'd cared more. Maybe you did. Maybe you just cared differently. Their brightness is the hook. Life felt lit up with them in it. Notice where your warmth goes when it isn't focused on one person. Friends, work, a hobby that's only yours. A candle that lights more than one corner doesn't burn out as fast, and doesn't have to wait for anyone else's light.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Jeong, you wanted to be first. That's a fair thing to want.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Byeong, replying to the group chat before your partner is a statement.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Same fire, different rooms. Next time, open the door between them.

jeong-fire.title: Two candles, both waiting
jeong-fire.text: You found someone who loved like you do: focused, deep, attentive to every detail. Your messages were long and careful. You both noticed a change in punctuation. For a while it felt like finally being read correctly. And then came the first real hurt, and both of you did the Jeong Fire thing: waited to be noticed. Nobody spoke first, because both of you expected the other to see it. The room went quiet and dark. Jealousy ran hot on both sides, because both of you love in an exclusive way, and a single like on someone else's photo could become a three-day atmosphere. Arguments were rare, but sharp, and both of you kept score in neat handwriting. You were so alike that neither of you could be the one to break the silence. The intensity is what you miss. Nobody else ever paid that much attention to you. Practise going first. Say 'I'm hurt' before you wait to be noticed. A candle that speaks up doesn't burn out alone in the dark.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: You loved each other so carefully. You just both waited to be found.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: A short reply is a busy day, not a verdict. Write it on your hand.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Go first. Say the feeling. It won't blow you out.

mu-earth.title: A lantern in the mountain temple
mu-earth.text: Your Mu Earth ex was the mountain your lantern hung in: steady, quiet, always there. You sent heartfelt, detailed messages; they replied briefly, but they always replied. You wanted feelings spoken out loud; they said 'it's fine' and meant it completely. When you were anxious, flickering, they often didn't notice until it had grown big, and then they were confused, because to them nothing had changed. Their stubbornness frustrated you. Your intensity puzzled them. You felt alone in the emotional work, while they felt they were doing everything right by simply staying. In a way, they were. Their reliability is what you miss. You never wondered whether they'd turn up, and that's rare for someone who worries as much as you do. Try reading reliability as love, everywhere in your life. The friend who always comes but never gushes. The parent who fixes things instead of saying things. Then ask plainly for one feeling word when you need it. People can learn to give what you name.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Mu, 'it's fine' is not an emotional update.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Jeong, they always showed up. That was their love letter.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: One feeling word per text. Not a speech. One word.

gi-earth.title: Candlelight in the kitchen, worrying
gi-earth.text: You and your Gi Earth ex were cosy in a way people envied: candles, home cooking, soft evenings in. But you were both worriers. You worried about feelings; they worried about practical things. 'Are we okay?' you'd ask. 'Did you eat?' they'd answer. Neither question got the answer it needed, so both of you kept worrying, together, in a slow spiral. Neither of you likes direct conflict, so resentments went quiet under the warmth. You felt they were too focused on tasks; they felt you were too focused on emotions. It was gentle and caring and still lonely, because you were reassuring each other in the wrong language. The care is what you miss. Soup when you were ill, a blanket you never asked for. Learn to answer the question underneath. When someone asks if you've eaten, they're asking if you're okay. When you ask if you're okay, say what you actually need. 'I need a hug, not a plan.' Clear words are kinder than gentle guessing.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Gi, 'did you eat?' is love. Say 'I love you' first, though.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Jeong, 'are we okay' forty times a week is a symptom, not a question.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Answer what they're actually asking. Then ask your own.

gyeong-metal.title: The candle and the steel
gyeong-metal.text: Your Gyeong Metal ex said things plainly, and you remembered every one of them for weeks. They were brief, decisive, a little rough. You were thoughtful and a little coded. When they said something blunt, it went deep and stayed there, flickering. When you hinted at what you needed, they missed it entirely and then got frustrated that you didn't just say it. You tried, gently, to soften their rough edges; they resented being improved. Fights were rarely loud, but they cut. And here's the strange part: they often forgot the fight by morning while you were still carrying it at lunch, and at dinner, and the next Tuesday. You were wounded by someone who didn't even know they'd swung. Their strength is what pulls. Next to them, you felt protected, and you liked how certain they were about everything. Say the actual thing. No codes, no hints. 'That comment hurt me.' Plain words aren't a betrayal of your softness. With steel, they're the only words that get through.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Gyeong, you forgot the fight by lunch. They're still on it. Know your audience.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Jeong, say the actual thing. Steel can't read candlelight.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Patient heat shapes metal. Silent heat just burns.

sin-metal.title: A flame near silver
sin-metal.text: It was beautiful and it scratched easily. Your Sin Metal ex had poise, taste, a way of moving through the world that made you want to be more careful. You loved intensely, and your intensity felt like pressure to them. Their critiques, small and precise, stung you more than they knew, because you take things personally and they say things precisely. Both of you are sensitive, and both of you withdraw when hurt. So tension simmered with nobody saying a word, and you reread their messages for clues, and they reread yours for the same. They found you possessive; you found them cold. Two delicate people tried not to break each other and broke things anyway. The elegance is the hook. Being loved by them felt like being chosen by someone with impeccable judgement. Lower the stakes. Send something silly. A bad selfie, a ridiculous meme. With careful people, the fastest way back to closeness is often a little bit of nonsense, offered without a speech attached.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Sin, you weren't cold. You were overwhelmed. Say that next time.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Jeong, rereading their text nine times doesn't decode it. Asking does.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: A silly selfie can melt a week of tension. Try it.

im-water.title: A lantern on the river
im-water.text: This was a Heavenly Combination, the lantern reflected on the river, and you felt it: a strange, deep recognition. Your Im Water ex was brilliant and restless and could talk about anything at 2am. You were warm and focused and wanted closeness. That's where the trouble lived. Their need for freedom made you anxious. Your need for closeness made them feel confined. You sent intimate, thoughtful messages; they replied in bursts, or with a philosophical essay at midnight, or not for a day. You got possessive; they disappeared; and the cycle repeated until neither of you could name where it started. It really was a meaningful match, and the pattern still won. That's hard to sit with. The depth is what pulls you. They saw your light and reflected it bigger. Trust rhythms instead of reading silences. Practise with friends first: when someone goes quiet, assume they're living their life, not leaving you. Anxiety is information about you, not proof about them.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Im, 'thinking of you' takes five seconds. You had five seconds.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Jeong, their silence was them being water. Not a goodbye.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: A great match with an anxious loop. Name the loop and it weakens.

gye-water.title: Rain on the candle
gye-water.text: Tender, sad-eyed, easily put out: that was the two of you. Your Gye Water ex was poetic and private and moody in a way that drew you in. You wanted clarity; they kept mysteries. You wanted to know what they were feeling; they needed not to be asked. When they were low, their mood could put out your flame entirely, and when you pressed for answers, it felt invasive to them. Both of you withdrew when hurt. So conflicts went silent and stayed unresolved, and long gaps in conversation began to feel like punishment, even when they weren't. You never quite got to the bottom of anything, and you're someone who needs to. The tenderness is what pulls you back. The good moments were so gentle they almost hurt. Let silence be allowed, but name what it means. 'I'm going quiet tonight, nothing's wrong.' Say it, and ask for the same. It won't remove the mystery from people. It will remove the dread.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Gye, 'it's not about you' is the kindest sentence for a worried candle.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Jeong, asking 'what's wrong' four times is not support.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Silence is allowed. Just not as a weapon.
